title: Kilwa: gold, coral and a city on an island
subtitle: An island city off the coast of today's Tanzania that grew rich on trade and was praised by a famous traveller. Even the dates of its rise are still being revised.

parts.text: Stories about African trade often stop at the Sahara. The Indian Ocean coast had its own trading cities.
Dhows set out from Kilwa and Sofala laden with gold, grain, wood and ivory.
Gold had traditionally been traded out of the port of Sofala.
As Kilwa grew rich, the city started to mint its own coins.

items.label: first coral buildings and coins, in recent excavation dating

parts.text: The excavation team places the first coral buildings and coins at the end of the tenth century; the older chronology had put the coins at the late twelfth.
That is why this page gives dates as its sources do, and does not give one figure for when Kilwa began.

image.caption: The ruins of Husuni Kubwa, the palace complex on Kilwa Kisiwani.
image.credit: Richard Mortel from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

parts.text: The sprawling fourteenth-century palace of Husuni Kubwa combined the roles of a fort, a castle and a warehouse.
Archaeology magazine describes it as a residence with some 100 rooms.
The fourteenth-century traveller Ibn Battuta called Kilwa one of the most beautiful towns in the world.

gaps: Left out for lack of a readable source outside Wikipedia and World History Encyclopedia: the size of Husuni Kubwa, the monolithic coral columns of the Great Mosque, tortoise shell and copper as exports, gold coming from Zimbabwe, and that the Portuguese attack left buildings in ruins.
The exact date of Ibn Battuta's visit (about 1331) is not confirmed by a source read here; National Geographic says only the fourteenth century.
The Metropolitan Museum and UNESCO pages on Kilwa could not be opened and are not cited.
The excavation chronology is an open-access manuscript in .docx form with no journal named; the published version should replace it.
No one from Tanzania has read this page yet.

keyPoints.text: Dhows set out from Kilwa and Sofala laden with gold, grain, wood and ivory.
Excavation dating places the first coral buildings and coins at the end of the tenth century, earlier than the late twelfth century in older work.
A fourteenth-century traveller, Ibn Battuta, called Kilwa one of the most beautiful towns in the world.
In 1505 Francisco de Almeida occupied Kilwa, bringing the sultanate to an end.
